title: Anthropic Says Sensitive AI Model Weights Were Not Accessed in Internal Breach
summary:
Anthropic confirmed that its core AI model weights, source code, and user conversations were not compromised during a recent penetration of its internal networks. The company disputed reports that the breach occurred in under 12 hours, stating that researchers from the startup Cathedral spent several days attempting to gain entry before exploiting vulnerabilities in two third-party software services.

The breach, which provided access to some of Anthropic's HR, sales, and IT systems, coincided with the company's filing for an initial public offering. Cathedral was founded by former staffers of the Department of Government Efficiency, and while Anthropic expressed gratitude for the findings, it stated that the activities were outside the scope of its bug bounty program's safe harbor policy.

selectedTweets.text:
Holy Moly. An AI cybersecurity startup founded by former DOGE staffers got into Anthropic's internal systems in under 12 hours using AI agents, The Washington Post reports.

The researchers found paths to meeting transcripts, salary and job-offer details, and Slack messages discussing Anthropic's advanced AI models after exploiting vulnerabilities in third-party business software.

Anthropic confirmed access to a limited set of sales, HR and IT systems, but said Claude conversations, source code and model weights were not accessed.

selectedTweets.text:
I think this story is important because it tells us about the future of cybersecurity (and of course what we can do better at Anthropic). But some of the Washington Post story / reaction on X is wrong. A few corrections:
- it didn’t take 12 hours. we saw several days of attempts. After these attempts, they exploited two 3rd party vulnerabilities, one they reported and the other we identified independently (and cut off access)
- nothing came close to our most sensitive systems, like model weights or Claude conversations
- this wasn't an ordinary bug bounty finding – this involved exploiting 3rd parties and accessing data. While this is unusual and out of scope of our safe harbor policy, we’re grateful these issues were found

From my researcher POV, the event is important because I'm concerned this is what the future will look like. Adversaries will use whatever models/tools they can. They’ll target everything with agents 24/7. They’ll hit your dependencies. I think models ~0.5-1 generations behind the current frontier can do this. And these are the dumbest models your adversaries will ever use!

So, what to do? You probably want to red team yourself all the time. Current models are *very* creative. I also think we should redesign software / systems so that you’re fundamentally less exposed. (We put out some research recently on formally verifying software and reducing attack surfaces; my mental model is basically “secure code is cheap to write now, so why not rewrite everything”)

> Anthropic has Mythos
> even unreleased versions 
> the world’s smartest cyber model
